answer_text:
Let  
\[
a_n=\lfloor \lambda n\rfloor .
\]
The given equation becomes
\[
2a_n=1-n+\lfloor \lambda a_n\rfloor,
\]
so
\[
\lfloor \lambda a_n\rfloor=2a_n+n-1. \tag{1}
\]

### 1. Necessity

Using \(\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1\) on (1),
\[
2a_n+n-1\le \lambda a_n<2a_n+n.
\]
Subtracting \(2a_n\),
\[
n-1\le (\lambda-2)a_n<n. \tag{2}
\]
Divide by \(n\):
\[
1-\frac1n\le (\lambda-2)\frac{a_n}{n}<1.
\]
Since \(a_n=\lfloor\lambda n\rfloor\), we have
\[
\frac{a_n}{n}\to \lambda \qquad (n\to\infty).
\]
Taking limits in the squeeze gives
\[
(\lambda-2)\lambda=1,
\]
so
\[
\lambda^2-2\lambda-1=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\lambda=1\pm\sqrt2.
\]
Because \(\lambda>0\) and (2) forces \(\lambda>2\), we must have
\[
\lambda=1+\sqrt2.
\]

### 2. Sufficiency

Let \(\lambda=1+\sqrt2\). Then
\[
\lambda-2=\sqrt2-1=\frac1\lambda.
\]
For any positive integer \(n\), set
\[
k=\lfloor \lambda n\rfloor.
\]
Since \(\lambda\) is irrational, the fractional part \(\{\lambda n\}\) satisfies
\[
0<\lambda n-k<1.
\]
Therefore
\[
n-1<\frac{k}{\lambda}=n-\frac{\lambda n-k}{\lambda}<n.
\]
Using \(\frac1\lambda=\lambda-2\),
\[
n-1<(\lambda-2)k<n.
\]
Adding \(2k\),
\[
2k+n-1<\lambda k<2k+n.
\]
Hence
\[
\lfloor \lambda k\rfloor=2k+n-1.
\]
Substituting back \(k=\lfloor\lambda n\rfloor\),
\[
\lfloor\lambda\lfloor\lambda n\rfloor\rfloor
=2\lfloor\lambda n\rfloor+n-1,
\]
which is exactly the required equation.

Thus the unique value is
\[
\boxed{1+\sqrt2}.
\]
